title: Portrait and Choir
premise: Xanthe Zhou, a reclusive urban explorer, has spent two decades rationalizing the sounds beneath her apartment building—until her sleep-recording rig captures a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud. The voice belongs to the Choir, a congregation sealed into the unmapped tunnels in 1974 by Xanthe's grandmother, who stole their founding relic to bind them. As the Choir's influence spreads through the building's tenants and the seal weakens, Xanthe must trace her grandmother's hidden past, recover the stolen reliquary, and descend to return it—learning that belonging was never something she could opt out of. In the flooded dark beneath the city, she offers herself as the Choir's final member, trading her solitude for theirs, and emerges changed: no longer invisible, no longer entirely alone in her own head.
about_author: A. M. Blackwood is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent years cataloguing condemned buildings before turning to fiction. Their work explores inherited guilt and the architecture of things left unsaid.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She maps a tunnel behind her apartment wall that appears on no city survey, telling herself the humming is HVAC resonance. Establishes her ritualized invisibility and meticulous documentation habits. Emotional beat: controlled unease—the reader sees what she refuses to.

chapters.title: Questions at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Reviewing sleep recordings for snoring data, she hears a second voice answering questions she never asked. She deletes the file, then recovers it from trash. Emotional beat: denial cracking; the first moment she speaks to the recording out loud—and it pauses, listening.

chapters.title: Tenants of the Deep Building
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with interludes from neighbor Mrs. Okafor. Residents begin humming the same four-note phrase; Mrs. Okafor says her late husband used to hum it too, before 1974. Emotional beat: creeping communal wrongness; Xanthe realizes she isn't the only one being reached.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Sorting her estranged grandmother's estate storage unit, she finds a locked reliquary-shaped case, a 1974 photograph of a congregation, and a deed to the building itself. Emotional beat: inheritance as burden; the family name on the deed reframes everything.

chapters.title: The Congregation of Saint Undersong
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV with archival documents. Newspaper clippings describe a church congregation that vanished mid-service in 1974; the building was sold weeks later to one Yuen Zhou. Emotional beat: dread hardening into purpose—her grandmother took something, and they want it back.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The recorded voice now addresses her directly, calling her 'keeper's blood,' asking when she will return what was taken. She answers on tape. Emotional beat: terror braided with a shameful thrill at finally being addressed, known, wanted.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okafor Sings
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okafor's POV. The neighbor walks into the basement stairwell at night singing the four notes; Xanthe pulls her back from a door that wasn't there yesterday. Emotional beat: love against duty—Xanthe breaks her own rule about involvement to save someone.

chapters.title: The Locksmith's Price
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A locksmith opens the reliquary case but flees without payment, leaving the inner box sealed with wax stamped by the vanished church. Emotional beat: isolation confirmed—even hired help won't stand near her now.

chapters.title: Yuen Zhou's Confession
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV reading a hidden letter. Her grandmother admits she took the Choir's reliquary to stop them 'singing the building down' and bound them with it, believing she saved the neighborhood. Emotional beat: grief and anger—her inheritance is a prison her grandmother built and never apologized for.

chapters.title: The Hum Moves Upstairs
chapters.summary: Multiple tenant POVs. The Choir's influence reaches the upper floors; walls sweat condensation in rhythm; a child draws the congregation's faces from memory. Emotional beat: siege atmosphere; the building itself is turning against its residents.

chapters.title: Descent Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She preps gear, maps the known tunnels, and records a goodbye video she deletes twice. The second voice gently corrects her route choices. Emotional beat: grim competence masking fear; she is planning her own funeral and knows it.

chapters.title: The Door That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Following the corrected route, she finds the sealed service door behind her own bedroom wall, warm to the touch, breathing faintly. Emotional beat: violation—the thing she hid from has been beside her bed for twenty years.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Grandmother Yuen's POV, epistolary/flashback chapter. The night of the sealing: the congregation sang the building's foundations loose, and Yuen stole the reliquary mid-rite, trapping them below as the tunnel collapsed. Emotional beat: tragic duty—a young woman's desperate choice becoming fifty years of silence.

chapters.title: Negotiation in the Dark
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the threshold, the Choir speaks through every tenant's mouth at once via phone calls, offering terms: return the reliquary, and the building goes quiet. Emotional beat: temptation—they promise her exactly what she always wanted: to be left alone, or to belong. They let her choose.

chapters.title: What the Reliquary Holds
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She breaks the wax seal: inside are not bones but names—handwritten vows of belonging from every congregant, including one signed 'Yuen Zhou.' Emotional beat: devastating reversal—her grandmother was meant to be the Choir's final member and fled her own vow.

chapters.title: The Building Remembers
chapters.summary: Tenant ensemble POV. The Choir stops waiting politely: doors open onto stairwells that descend instead of rise, and residents begin sleepwalking toward the basement. Xanthe barricades the stairwell with Mrs. Okafor. Emotional beat: deadline pressure—the choice is being taken from her.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Xanthe and Mrs. Okafor's alternating POV. Mrs. Okafor reveals her husband was a congregant who escaped the sealing and spent his life humming homesick; she asks Xanthe to carry his name down with her. Emotional beat: tenderness in extremis—belonging offered freely, which changes what returning the reliquary means.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She carries the reliquary through flooding tunnels past pews grown from concrete, toward the collapsed nave where the Choir has waited fifty years, patient and starving. Emotional beat: awe and terror fused; the horror is also, horribly, a homecoming.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She returns the reliquary and reads the vows aloud; the Choir begins to dissolve into release rather than rage—but the binding needs a keeper's blood to complete, and the exit is already underwater. Emotional beat: sacrifice accepted without melodrama; she signs her own name.

chapters.title: Choir
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, submerged and transformed. She joins the song—not consumed but harmonized—and the Choir, completed, lets the building stand. The waters recede. Emotional beat: transcendence within horror; belonging achieved at the cost of selfhood, and somehow worth it.

chapters.title: Quiet Building
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okafor's POV, three months later. Tenants remember nothing; the tunnels are gone from every survey again. Only Mrs. Okafor, holding her husband's returned vow page, sometimes hears four notes from the wall—and hums the fifth back. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace; mourning and gratitude entangled.

chapters.title: Keeper's Blood
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, coda. Living between worlds now, she keeps the building's archive, hears the Choir when she chooses, and adds new names to the reliquary for those who ask to belong. Final line mirrors the opening recording: a question asked, an answer given. Emotional beat: resolution as ongoing covenant—invisibility traded, willingly, for voice.
